paragraphs.text: <smallcaps>A memorial </smallcaps> a which Ambrose, a chief man of Greece, wrote: who became a Christian, and all his fellow-senators raised an outcry against him; and he fled from them, and wrote and pointed out to them all their foolishness.
Beginning his discourse, he answered and said:—

Think not, men of Greece, that my separation from your customs has been made without a just and proper reason. For I acquainted myself with all your wisdom, consisting of poetry, of oratory, of philosophy; and when I found not there anything agreeable to what is right, or that is worthy of the divine nature, I resolved to make myself acquainted with the wisdom of the Christians also, and to learn and see who they are, and when they took their rise, and what is the nature of this new and strange wisdom of theirs, or on what good hopes those who are imbued with it rely, that they speak only that which is true.

Men of Greece, when I came to examine the Christian writings, I found not any folly in them, as I had found in the celebrated Homer, who has said concerning the wars of the two trials: Because of Helen, many of the Greeks perished at Troy, away from their beloved home. For, first of all, we are told concerning Agamemnon their king, that by reason of the foolishness of his brother Menelaus, and the violence of his madness, and the uncontrollable nature of his passion, he resolved to go and rescue Helen from the hands of a certain leprous shepherd; and afterwards, when the Greeks had become victorious in the war, and burnt cities, and taken women and children captive, and the land was filled with blood, and the rivers with corpses, Agamemnon himself also was found to be taken captive by his passion for Briseis. Patroclus, again, we are told, was slain, and Achilles, the son of the goddess Thetis, mourned over him; Hector was dragged along the ground, and Priam and Hecuba together were weeping over the loss of their children; Astyanax, the son of Hector, was thrown down from the walls of Ilion, and his mother Andromache the mighty Ajax bore away into captivity; and that which was taken as booty was after a little while, all squandered in sensual indulgence.

Of the wiles of Odysseus the son of Laertes, and of his murders, who shall tell the tale? For of a hundred and ten suitors did his house in one day become the grave, and it was filled with corpses and blood. He, too, it was that by his wickedness gained the praises of men, because through his pre-eminence in craft he escaped detection; he, too, it was who, you say, sailed upon the sea, and heard not the voice of the Sirens only because he stopped his ears with wax.

The famous Achilles, again, the son of Peleus, who bounded across the river, and routed the Trojans, and slew Hector—this said hero of yours became the slave of Philoxena, and was overcome by an Amazon as she lay dead and stretched upon her bier; and he put off his armour, and arrayed himself in nuptial garments, and finally fell a sacrifice to love.

Thus much concerning your great men; and you, Homer, had deserved forgiveness, if your silly story-telling had gone so far only as to prate about men, and not about the gods. As for what he says about the gods, I am ashamed even to speak of it: for the stories that have been invented about them are very wicked and shocking; passing strange, too, and not to be believed; and, if the truth must be told, fit only to be laughed at. For a person will be compelled to laugh when he meets with them, and will not believe them when he hears them. For think of gods who did not one of them observe the laws of rectitude, or of purity, or of modesty, but were adulterers, and spent their time in debauchery, and yet were not condemned to death, as they ought to have been!

Why, the sovereign of the gods, the very father of gods and men, not only, as you say, was an adulterer (this was but a light thing), but even slew his own father, and was a pederast. I will first of all speak of his adultery, though I blush to do so: for he appeared to Antiope as a satyr, and descended upon Danaë as a shower of gold, and became a bull for Europa, and a swan for Leda; while the love of Semele, the mother of Dionysus, exposed both his own ardency of passion and the jealousy of the chaste Hera. Ganymede the Phrygian, too, he carried off disguised as an eagle, that the fair and comely boy, forsooth, might serve as cup-bearer to him. This said sovereign of the gods, moreover killed his father Kronos, that he might seize upon his kingdom.

Oh! To how many charges is the sovereign of the gods amenable, and how many deaths does he deserve to die, as an adulterer, and as a sorcerer, and as a pederast! Read to the sovereign of the gods, O men of Greece, the law concerning parricide, and the condemnation pronounced on adultery, and about the shame that attaches to the vile sin of pederasty. How many adulterers has the sovereign of the gods indoctrinated in sin! Nay, how many pederasts, and sorcerers, and murderers! So that, if a man be found indulging his passions, he must not be put to death: because he has done this that he may become like the sovereign of the gods; and, if he be found a murderer, he has an excuse in the sovereign of the gods; and, if a man be a sorcerer, he has learned it from the sovereign of the gods; and, if he be a pederast, the sovereign of the gods is his apologist. Then, again, if one should speak of courage, Achilles was more valiant that this said sovereign of the gods: for he slew the man that slew his friend; but the sovereign of the gods wept over Sarpedon his son when he was dying, being distressed for him.

Pluto, again, who is a god, carried off Kora, and the mother of Kora was hurrying here and there searching for her daughter in all desert places; and, although Alexander Paris, when he had carried off Helen, paid the penalty of vengeance, as having made himself her lover by force, yet Pluto, who is a god, when he carried off Kora, remained without rebuke; and, although Menelaus, who is a man, knew how to search for Helen his wife, yet Demeter, who is a goddess, knew not where to search for Kora her daughter.

Let Hephæstus put away jealousy from him, and not indulge resentment. For he was hated, because he was old and lame; while Ares was loved, because he was a youth and beautiful in form. There was, however, a reproof administered in respect of the adultery. Hephæstus was not, indeed, at first aware of the love existing between Venus his wife and Ares; but, when he did become acquainted with it, Hephæstus said: Come, see a ridiculous and senseless piece of behaviour— how to me, who am her own, Venus, the daughter of the sovereign of the gods, is offering insult— to me, I say, who am her own, and is paying honour to Ares, who is a stranger to her. But to the sovereign of the gods it was not displeasing: for he loved such as were like these. Penelope, moreover, remained a widow twenty years, because she was expecting the return of her husband Odysseus, and busied herself with cunning tasks, and persevered in works of skill, while all those suitors kept pressing her to marry them; but Venus, who is a goddess, when Hephæstus her husband was close to her, deserted him, because she was overcome by love for Ares. Hearken, men of Greece: which of you would have dared to do this, or would even have endured to see it? And, if any one should dare to act so, what torture would be in store for him, or what scourgings!

Kronos, again, who is a god, who devoured all those children of his, was not even brought before a court of justice. They further tell us that the sovereign of the gods, his son, was the only one that escaped from him; and that the madness of Kronos his father was cheated of its purpose because Rhea his wife, the mother of the sovereign of the gods, offered him a stone in the place of the said sovereign of the gods, his son, to prevent him from devouring him. Hearken, men of Greece, and reflect upon this madness! Why, even the dumb animal that grazes in the field knows its proper food, and does not touch strange food; the wild beast, too, and the reptile, and the bird, know their food. As for men, I need not say anything about them: ye yourselves are acquainted with their food, and understand it well. But Kronos, who is a god, not knowing his proper food, ate up a stone!

Therefore, O men of Greece, if you will have such gods as these, do not find fault with one another when you do such-like things. Be not angry with your son when he forms the design to kill you: because he thus resembles the sovereign of the gods. And, if a man commit adultery with your wife, why do you think of him as an enemy, and yet to the sovereign of the gods, who is like him, doest worship and service? Why, too, do you find fault with your wife when she has committed adultery and leads a dissolute life, and yet payest honour to Venus, and placest her images in shrines? Persuade your Solon to repeal his laws; Lycurgus, also, to make no laws; let the Areopagus repeal theirs, and judge no more; and let the Athenians have councils no longer. Let the Athenians discharge Socrates from his office: for no one like Kronos has ever come before him. Let them not put to death Orestes, who killed his mother: for, lo! The sovereign of the gods did worse things than these to his father. Œdipus also too hastily inflicted mischief on himself, in depriving his eyes of sight, because he had killed his mother unwittingly: for he did not think about the sovereign of the gods, who killed his father and yet remained without punishment. Medea, again, who killed her children, the Corinthians banish from their country; and yet they do service and honour to Kronos, who devoured his children. Then, too, as regards Alexander Paris— he was right in carrying off Helen: for he did it that he might become like Pluto, who carried off Kora. Let your men be set free from law, and let your cities be the abode of wanton women, and a dwelling-place for sorcerers.

Wherefore, O men of Greece, seeing that your gods are grovelling like yourselves, and your heroes destitute of courage, as your dramas tell and your stories declare— then, again, what shall be said of the tribulations of Orestes; and the couch of Thyestes; and the foul taint in the family of Pelops; and concerning Danaus, who through jealousy killed his sons- in-law, and deprived them of offspring; the banquet of Thyestes, too, feeding upon the corpse set before him by way of vengeance for her whom he had wronged; about Procne also, to this hour screaming as she flies; her sister too, warbling, with her tongue cut out? What, moreover, is it fitting to say about the murder committed by Œdipus, who took his own mother to wife, and whose brothers killed one another, they being at the same time his sons?

Your festivals, too, I hate; for there is no moderation where they are; the sweet flutes also, dispellers of care, which play as an incitement to dancing; and the preparation of ointments, wherewith ye anoint yourselves; and the chaplets which you put on. In the abundance of your wickedness, too, you have forgotten shame, and your understandings have become blinded, and you have been infuriated by the heat of passion, and have loved the adulterous bed.

Had these things been said by another, perhaps our adversaries would have brought an accusation against him, on the plea that they were untrue. But your own poets say them, and your own hymns and dramas declare them.

Come, therefore, and be instructed in the word of God, and in the wisdom which is fraught with comfort. Rejoice, and become partakers of it. Acquaint yourselves with the King Immortal, and acknowledge His servants. For not in arms do they make their boast, nor do they commit murders: because our Commander has no delight in abundance of strength, nor yet in horsemen and their gallant array, nor yet in illustrious descent; but He delights in the pure soul, fenced round by a rampart of righteousness. The word of God, moreover, and the promises of our good King, and the works of God, are ever teaching us. Oh the blessedness of the soul that is redeemed by the power of the word! Oh the blessedness of the trumpet of peace without war! Oh the blessedness of the teaching which quenches the fire of appetite! Which, though it makes not poets, nor fits men to be philosophers, nor has among its votaries the orators of the crowd; yet instructs men, and makes the dead not to die, and lifts men from the earth as gods up to the region which is above the firmament. Come, be instructed, and be like me: for I too was once as you are.

latex.p0003: \Emph{纪念}，由盎博罗削这位希腊的主要人物写成：他成为了一名基督徒，而他所有的元老同僚都对他提出抗议；于是他逃离他们，写下了这些文字，向他们指出他们所有的愚昧。
latex.p0004: 他开始他的讲论，回答说：——
latex.p0005: 希腊人啊，不要以为我脱离你们的习俗是没有公正合理的原因的。因为我熟知你们的全部智慧，\Emph{包含}诗词、演说、哲学；当我在其中找不到任何\Emph{在那里}\Emph{合乎正义的}事物，或什么配得上神性的事物时，我便决心也去了解基督徒的智慧，并学习去认识他们\Emph{是谁}，\Emph{他们是何时兴起的}，以及他们这种新奇而陌生的智慧\Emph{的本质}是什么，或者那些接受它的人是依靠什么美好的\Emph{希望}，使他们\Emph{只}说真话。
latex.p0006: 希腊人啊，当我开始考察\Emph{基督徒的著作}时，我发现其中没有任何\Emph{愚蠢之处}，如同我在著名的荷马那里发现的一样，他曾论及两次战争的冲突说：\Quote{因为海伦，许多希腊人在特洛伊丧身，远离他们心爱的家园。}因为，首先，我们得知关于他们的国王阿伽门农，由于他兄弟墨涅拉俄斯的愚蠢、他疯狂的暴力和不可控制的激情，他决定去从一个麻风牧羊人\Emph{的手}中救回海伦；\Emph{后来}，当希腊人在战争中得胜、烧毁城市、俘虏妇女和孩童、遍地是血、河中满是尸体时，阿伽门农自己也被发现被\Emph{他对}布里塞伊斯的激情所俘虏。再者，我们得知帕特罗克洛斯被杀，女神忒提斯之子阿喀琉斯为他哀悼；赫克托耳被\Emph{拖在地上}，普里阿摩斯和赫卡柏一起为失去儿女而哭泣；赫克托耳的儿子阿斯提阿那克斯从特洛伊城墙上被扔下，他的母亲安德洛玛刻被强大的埃阿斯\Emph{俘虏}；而所掠得的战利品不久之后\Emph{全部}浪费在感官享乐中。
latex.p0007: 至于拉埃尔特斯之子奥德修斯的诡计和谋杀，谁能尽述呢？因为他的房子在一天之内成了一百一十个求婚者的坟墓，充满了尸体和血。也\Emph{正是}他，因他的邪恶得到了\Emph{人们的}赞美，因为他凭借\Emph{他的}诡计高明而逃脱了发现；也\Emph{正是}他，你们说他航行海上，只因为他用蜡封住耳朵才\Emph{没有}听到塞壬的歌声\Emph{而已}。
latex.p0008: 再者，著名的阿喀琉斯，珀琉斯之子，他曾跳过河流，击溃特洛伊人，杀死赫克托耳——你们所说的这位英雄成了菲洛克塞娜的奴隶，并被一个亚马逊女战士战胜，当时她\Emph{躺着}死了，\Emph{伸展在灵床上}；他脱掉铠甲，穿上婚服，最终成了爱情的牺牲品。
latex.p0009: 关于你们\Emph{的}伟大\Quote{人物}就说这些吧；而你，荷马，如果你那些愚蠢的胡说仅限于谈论人，而不涉及众神，你本应得到宽恕。至于他\Emph{所说}关于众神的话，我甚至羞于启齿：因为那些编造出来的关于他们的故事极其邪恶和令人震惊；也极其奇怪且不可信；并且，如果必须说出真相，只配被嘲笑。因为一个人遇到它们时\Emph{不得不}发笑，听到它们时也不相信。因为\Emph{想想}那些神祇，他们没有一位遵守正直、纯洁或谦逊的法则，反而\Emph{都是}通奸者，沉溺于放荡，\Emph{然而}却没有被判处死刑，这是他们罪有应得的！
latex.p0010: 哎呀，众神之王，就是那位\Quote{众神与人类的父亲}，不仅如你们所说是个通奸者（这还算小事），甚至还杀了自己的父亲，并且是个娈童者。我将首先谈论\Emph{他的}通奸，尽管我\Emph{这样做}会脸红：因为他以萨提尔的模样出现在安提俄珀面前，化作一阵金雨降在达那厄身上，为了欧罗巴变成一头公牛，为勒达变成一只天鹅；而狄俄尼索斯之母塞墨勒的爱情既暴露了他\Emph{激情的}热烈，也暴露了贞洁赫拉的嫉妒。此外，他还\Emph{伪装}成一只鹰拐走了弗里吉亚人伽倪墨得斯，让这个美貌俊俏的男孩可以给他当酒童。这位众神之王还杀死了他的父亲克洛诺斯，以便夺取他的王国。
latex.p0011: 哦！众神之王该当多少项指控，该当多少\Emph{次}死刑，作为一个通奸者、巫觋和娈童者！希腊人啊，向众神之王宣读关于弑父的法律、对通奸的判决以及\Emph{关于}附属于男色这卑劣之罪的羞耻。众神之王已经使多少通奸者\Emph{在罪中}受到教化！不仅如此，多少娈童者、巫觋和谋杀者！所以，如果有人被发现放纵情欲，他不应被处死：因为他这样做是要变得像众神之王；如果他被发现是谋杀者，他有借口\Emph{在于}众神之王；如果一个人是巫觋，他是从众神之王学来的；如果他是娈童者，众神之王是他的辩护者。再者，如果要说勇敢，阿喀琉斯比这位所谓的众神之王更勇敢：因为他杀死了杀死他朋友的人；但众神之王却为他临死的儿子萨耳珀冬哭泣，\Emph{为他}忧伤。
latex.p0012: 再者，那个为神的\Person{普路托}掠走了\Person{科拉}，\Person{科拉}的母亲奔波各处，在一切荒芜之地寻找她的女儿；\Emph{尽管}亚历山大·帕里斯在掠走\Person{海伦}之后，因\Emph{使自己}强占了她的恋人而受到了报复的惩罚，但身为神的\Person{普路托}掠走\Person{科拉}之后却未受指责；\Emph{尽管}身为人的\Person{墨涅拉俄斯}知道如何寻找他的妻子\Person{海伦}，但身为女神的\Person{得墨忒耳}却不知何处寻找她的女儿\Person{科拉}。
latex.p0013: 让\Person{赫菲斯托斯}除掉嫉妒，不要心怀怨恨。因为他因年老和跛足而被憎恨；而\Person{阿瑞斯}因年轻貌美而被爱。然而，关于通奸一事，确有一番\Emph{属于}斥责\Emph{的言论}。起初，\Person{赫菲斯托斯}并不知道他的妻子\Person{维纳斯}与\Person{阿瑞斯}之间的恋情；但当他知晓后，\Person{赫菲斯托斯}说：\Quote{来，看看一件荒唐无知的行为——\Person{维纳斯}，众神之王的女儿，竟如何辱慢我，她的丈夫——我\Emph{说}，她的丈夫，却向与她无亲的\Person{阿瑞斯}表示尊崇。}但这对众神之王来说并不令他不悦：因为他喜爱像这样的人。此外，\Person{佩涅洛佩}守寡二十年，因为她期盼丈夫\Person{奥德修斯}\Emph{归来}，忙于巧计，坚持不懈地从事技艺之作，而所有那些求婚者不断逼迫她\Emph{嫁给他们}；但身为女神的\Person{维纳斯}，在丈夫\Person{赫菲斯托斯}近在咫尺时，竟离弃了他，因她被对\Person{阿瑞斯}的爱所征服。希腊人啊，请听：你们中有谁敢做这事，或甚至容忍看见这事？如果有人\Quote{敢}\Emph{如此行}，等待他的将是何等酷刑，或何等鞭打！
latex.p0014: 再者，那个为神的\Person{克洛诺斯}，吞噬了所有那些\Emph{他的}孩子，甚至没有被带上法庭。他们又告诉\Emph{我们}，众神之王——他的儿子——是唯一逃脱他的；而他的父亲\Person{克洛诺斯}的疯狂被欺骗\Emph{了其目的}，因为\Person{瑞亚}——他的妻子、众神之王的母亲——在那位众神之王——他的儿子——的位置上提供了一块石头，以防止他吞噬他。希腊人啊，请听，请反思这疯狂！\Emph{连}那在田间吃草的哑巴动物都知道它\Emph{应有的}食物，不碰陌生的食物；野兽、爬虫和飞鸟都知道它们的食物。至于人，我无需多言：你们自己熟悉他们的食物，且\Emph{十分}理解。但身为神的\Person{克洛诺斯}，不知他\Emph{应有的}食物，竟吞噬了一块石头！
latex.p0015: 因此，希腊人啊，若你们有这般的众神，就不要在彼此行类似之事时互相指责。不要因你儿子图谋杀你而向他发怒：因为他\Emph{如此}像众神之王。若有人与你的妻子通奸，为何你视他为仇敌，却对与他相像的众神之王献上敬拜事奉？再者，为何你因妻子犯了通奸、生活放荡而指责她，\Emph{却}向\Person{维纳斯}致敬，并将她的\Emph{像}置于神龛中？说服\Emph{你们的}\Person{梭伦}废除他的法律；也说服\Person{吕库古}不再立法；让\Person{阿雷奥帕古斯}废除他们的法律，不再审判；让雅典人不再有议事会。让雅典人将\Person{苏格拉底}\Emph{解职}：因为从未有像\Person{克洛诺斯}的人\Emph{曾}出现在他面前。让他们不要处死杀母的\Person{俄瑞斯忒斯}：因为看哪！众神之王对他的父亲行了比这更恶的事。\Person{俄狄浦斯}也\Emph{过于}仓促地自招祸患，剥夺了自己的视力，因他无意中杀了母亲：因为他没有考虑众神之王——他杀了自己的父亲却\Emph{仍}未受惩罚。再者，\Person{美狄亚}杀了自己的孩子，科林斯人将她\Emph{驱逐出境}；\Emph{然而}他们却事奉并尊崇吞噬了自己孩子的\Person{克洛诺斯}。再者，关于亚历山大·帕里斯——他掠走\Person{海伦}是对的：\Emph{因为他这样做}是为了变得像掠走\Person{科拉}的\Person{普路托}。让\Emph{你们的}人摆脱法律，让\Emph{你们的}城市成为荡妇\Emph{的居所}和巫师的住处。
latex.p0016: 因此，希腊人啊，既然你们的众神像你们一样卑微，你们的英雄缺乏勇气，正如你们的戏剧所讲述、你们的故事所宣告——那么，\Emph{又该说些什么}关于\Person{俄瑞斯忒斯}的苦难，关于\Person{堤厄斯忒斯}的床榻，关于\Person{珀罗普斯}\Emph{家族}的污秽玷染，关于\Person{达那俄斯}——他因嫉妒杀了他的女婿们，夺去了他们的后裔；还有\Person{堤厄斯忒斯}的宴席，\Emph{吞食}那具\Emph{作为报复而摆在他面前的}他所\Emph{错待}之人的\Emph{尸体}；关于\Person{普罗克涅}——她至今仍在飞翔中尖叫；她的妹妹——舌头被割，啁啾鸣唱？再者，关于\Person{俄狄浦斯}所犯的凶杀——他娶了自己的母亲\Emph{为妻}，而他的兄弟们——\Emph{同时}也是他的儿子——互相残杀，又该说些什么？
latex.p0017: 你们的节庆，我也憎恨；因为其中毫无节制；还有那甜美的笛声，驱散忧虑，奏起作为舞蹈的激励；以及膏油的预备，你们用以涂抹自身；还有你们戴的花冠。在你们邪恶的丰盈中，你们也忘记了羞耻，你们的心智变得盲目，你们被\Emph{情欲}的狂热所激怒，爱上了通奸的床榻。
latex.p0018: 若这些话由别人说出，或许\Emph{我们的对手}会提出控告，\Emph{声称}它们不真实。但你们的诗人自己说了这些话，你们的赞美诗和戏剧也宣告了它们。
latex.p0019: 所以，来，接受天主的圣言和充满安慰的智慧的教导。欢喜吧，并成为它的分享者。认识那不朽的君王，并承认祂的仆人们。因为他们并不以武器夸耀，也不实行谋杀：因为我们的统帅并不喜悦力量的丰盛，也不喜悦骑兵和他们华丽的阵列，也不喜悦显赫的出身；祂所喜悦的是纯洁的灵魂，被正义的壁垒所围绕。此外，天主的圣言、我们良善君王的应许以及天主的工程，不断教导我们。哦，那藉着圣言的力量而得救的灵魂是\Emph{有福的}！哦，那没有战争的和平号角是\Emph{有福的}！哦，那熄灭欲望之火的教导是\Emph{有福的}！这教导，\Emph{虽然}不造就诗人，也不使\Emph{人}成为哲学家，在\Emph{其追随者中}也没有群众的演说家；却教导\Emph{人}，使死者不再死亡，并将人从地上提升，\Emph{如同神祇}，升到穹苍之上的领域。来，受教导，成为像我一样：因为我也曾\Emph{一度}像你们一样。
